replying_to: Replying to Token Pruning Meets Audio: Investigating Unique Behaviors in Vision Transformer-Based Audio Classification
display_title: Official Review of Submission9332 by Reviewer pSH5

summary.value: The authors propose the MP-EViT model, which is the first time the token pruning technique is applied to the Vision Transformer-based audio classification task. A comprehensive experimental analysis reveals the unique token pruning patterns in audio classification, proves the importance of background tokens, and significantly reduces the amount of computation while maintaining high accuracy.

strengths.value:
1. For the first time, token pruning is applied to the audio classification task, and its unique behavioral patterns are deeply analyzed. This opens up a new research direction for the efficient application of ViT in the audio domain.

2. This study provides an important efficiency optimization scheme for the application of ViT in the audio domain, and reveals the unique characteristics of audio data processing, which is of great significance in promoting the development of audio AI.

3. The authors demonstrate through a large number of ablation experiments that what token pruning focuses on in the speech domain is dramatically different from that in the image domain, and analyze the reasons for this.

weaknesses.value:
1. The experimental dataset and model scale are relatively limited. The study utilized only the SPC-2 and ESC-50 datasets, and the ViT-B configuration was exclusively employed. Expanding the experimental scope could provide more comprehensive insights. It is recommended to conduct experiments on additional audio classification tasks, such as emotion recognition and speaker identification, to validate the generalizability of the proposed method.

2. There is a lack of comparison with other audio classification methods. The manuscript primarily compares the proposed method with baseline models, without assessing performance against other state-of-the-art audio classification techniques. This omission makes it difficult to comprehensively evaluate the advantages of the proposed approach. Has consideration been given to comparing token pruning with other model compression techniques, such as knowledge distillation and quantization?

3. The explanation of the mechanism for retaining background tokens is insufficiently detailed. While experiments demonstrate the significance of background tokens, the analysis of the underlying mechanisms that lead the model to preferentially retain these tokens is not adequately explored.

4. The manuscript mentions that due to resource constraints, only the ViT-B configuration was employed. Could supplementary small-scale experiments be conducted to investigate the impact of model capacity on the pruning strategy?

5. Is it possible to extend the use of mel spectrograms to magnitude spectrograms? This is particularly relevant, as magnitude spectrograms are more widely utilized in the field of speech processing.

questions.value: The contents are the same as Weaknesses.

confidence.description: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.

summary.value: The paper propose token pruning in Vision transformers fed with spectrograms for audio based classification tasks. Authors prune tokens which are least attended by the other tokens. The paper shows that token pruning can lead to less computation with very minimal drop in accuracy. Authors further show that unlike vision, for audio tasks background tokens are also being retained thereby showing their importance for such tasks.

strengths.value: The paper presents a novel application of token pruning techniques by applying them in audio classifications tasks. The presentation of this paper is clear and it is easy to read. Authors also provide various analysis providing insights on the nature of token pruning for such tasks showing that background tokens can also be important for audio tasks. Moreover, on the two datasets considered in the paper, authors show almost no drop in accuracy while reducing MAC operations significantly.

weaknesses.value:
1. ViTs are very data hungry. The size of datasets considered is not that huge. This combined with high accuracy values in Table 1 could indicate model may be over-fitting to tasks or datasets at hand. Have authors tried to train the model on a bigger dataset e.g. Audioset and then evaluate its performance on other audio classification tasks such as the two mentioned in paper (SPC-v2 and ESC-50). Authors should show better generalizability of their proposed approach to make their claims stronger.

 2. The proposed approach reduces tokens from one layer to next similar to downsampling. Have the authors compared their proposed approach with other operations such as averaging blocks of n-tokens, uniform downsampling, downsampling by picking tokens randomly to name a few.

Also, since audio MAE uses mean pooling, it is kind of intuitive that CLS-EViT will work worse than MP-EViT. A better comparison would be against CLS-EViT of AST (since AST uses CLS token for classification) and MP-EViT of Audi-MAE

comment.value:
The primary challenge is the loss of accuracy when tokens are pruned at every layer. On top of that, frequent token pruning can slow down single-batch inference which could be a problem for service deployment.
When measuring throughput of ESC-50 with a batch size of 128 using an RTX 4090, as the same way in our paper, the results are as follows:


	Keep-rate 0.5, pruning at locations 4th / 7th / 10th:
	MAC (G): 11.37, Throughput (samples/s): 1264
	Keep-rate 0.9, pruning at every layer:
	MAC (G): 12.95, Throughput (samples/s): 1102
	Keep-rate 0.8, pruning at every layer:
	MAC (G): 7.83, Throughput (samples/s): 1795

Below are the results for inference with a batch size of 1:

	Without token pruning:
	MAC (G): 23.11, Throughput (samples/s): 365
	Keep-rate 0.5, pruning at locations 4th / 7th / 10th:
	MAC (G): 11.37, Throughput (samples/s): 487
	Keep-rate 0.9, pruning at every layer:
	MAC (G): 12.95, Throughput (samples/s): 412
	Keep-rate 0.8, pruning at every layer:
	MAC (G): 7.83, Throughput (samples/s): 420

Throughput degradation occurs because tensor memory operations caused by pruning cannot be effectively amortized when using a batch size of 1.

display_title: Official Review of Submission9332 by Reviewer nrYL

summary.value: The authors applied a token pruning method originally used in vision tasks to audio classification, successfully reducing MAC operations and improving throughput with minimal accuracy loss. While the experiments were limited to only two datasets (SPC-2 and ESC-50), making the scope somewhat narrow, the detailed analysis provided valuable insights.

strengths.value:
I think the strength of the paper lies in its discussion and ablation studies.

Until Section 3.4, I thought it was merely applying a pruning method in ViT directly to audio classification, which, in my opinion, makes the contribution fall below the ICLR bar. However, the discussion and ablation study that follow are much more interesting than the proposed pruning method. I am a bit surprised that "background" patches are attended. So it brings some new knowledge to me.

weaknesses.value:
There are a few major flaws:

1- Audio MAE is a special Transformer model that is trained with Masked Data Modeling, i.e., it learns to attend to minimal patches by design. Thus, the conclusion of this paper is conditioned on a special MAE model, or the general Transformer model is questionable. This is a fatal issue and needs to be either clarified or experiments added on Transformers trained without MAE (e.g., the original AST). I cannot recommend acceptance without fixing this.

2- The pruning method is almost the same as the vision version, which is not novel enough.

3- The discussion is interesting, but for non-trivial conclusions, we also need to be careful. Why -0.65 (is that dB?) is a good measure of signal and background? If I remember correctly, speech commands are mostly clean speech, so the low intensity might be just some consonants / vowel transitions. Also, it is just 10-32 keywords classification; the model does not need to attend to everything (in contrast, doing large vocab ASR needs). So, more fine-tuning datasets are also needed.

In general, the discussions in the paper are interesting and can be the basis of a good paper, but a lot of further work needs to be done before publication.

* To see if our study works for general transformer models, we added token pruning experiments using the original AST. Additionally, we acquired the AudioSet-2M dataset and pretrained AST with mean pooling. With a keep-rate of 0.5 (pruning half of the tokens at each stage), the accuracy drops by 0.2% on the SPC-2 dataset and 0.5% on the ESC-50 dataset when using a [CLS] token, and by 0.2% on SPC-2 and 1.0% on ESC-50 when using mean pooling for classification.

* Interestingly, the tokens retained by AST contain more signal information than those retained by AudioMAE. We found this to be a distinct characteristic of AST, regardless of the summarization method (CLS token or mean pooling). Unlike AudioMAE results, AST gives much higher attention scores to the signal tokens than to the background token. And the pruning patterns of AudioMAE and AST are notably different. We added detailed comparison including visualization results to the appendix of our revised paper.

* This difference can be attributed to their pretraining objectives: In AudioMAE, the model processes audio by considering not only signal but also background tokens, as all patches are masked during training. In contrast, AST focuses primarily on signal tokens with higher intensity values. This distinction can lead to different pruning behaviors: AudioMAE-TopK pruning retains both signal and background tokens for classification tasks, while AST-TopK pruning primarily preserves signal tokens.

* Before submission, we thought that the vanilla AST, trained with supervised learning, was outdated, as methods like MAE or bootstrap learning have shown better performance on various benchmarks (especially on speaker identification task, VoxCeleb-1). Thank you for pointing this out; your review enabled us to do additional ablation studies and uncover new pruning patterns.

2. The pruning method is almost the same as the vision version, which is not novel enough.

* Our main contribution is analyzing token pruning in depth rather than emphasizing the idea of applying token pruning to audio tasks.

* We began our research using the original EViT. But, to clarify the origin of tokens for analysis, we disabled fusing inattentive tokens. In our revision, following the work of (J. B. Haurum et al, 2023) [1] we renamed our model to AudioMAE-TopK because we are not using token merging features.

3. The discussion is interesting, but for non-trivial conclusions, we also need to be careful. Why -0.65 (is that dB?) is a good measure of signal and background? If I remember correctly, speech commands are mostly clean speech, so the low intensity might be just some consonants / vowel transitions. Also, it is just 10-32 keywords classification; the model does not need to attend to everything (in contrast, doing large vocab ASR needs). So, more fine-tuning datasets are also needed.
* As shown in Figure 4, -0.65 is a normalized intensity value not a dB unit. During the rebuttal period, we experimented with two more datasets: VoxCeleb-1 for speaker identification tasks and AudioSet-20K for general audio classification. After checking their distribution intensity values, as the reviewer suggested, we found that the histograms’ distributions differ from those of SPC-2 and ESC-50. We set the signal threshold to -1.25 for VoxCeleb-1 and -1.0 for AudioSet-20K.
* In VoxCeleb-1, the accuracy dropped by 0.4% at a keep-rate of 0.7. For AudioSet-20K, the mean Average Precision (mAP) decreased by approximately 0.005 for every 0.1 reduction in the keep-rate, until it reached a keep-rate of 0.6.
* A recent work of token pruning in image classification task (Liu et al., 2024a) [2] shows tokens from the target object play an important role in the prediction results. If these tokens are pruned, the accuracy drops. When token pruning is applied to image classification tasks, one can assess whether a token pruning method works well by considering the masked region of an object and checking which tokens are pruned.

* To the best of our knowledge, there is no straightforward way to quantify how much crucial information a token carries in general audio classification tasks. Therefore, it is difficult to determine whether the model performs pruning effectively by merely observing the pruning pattern. We couldn’t create a mask covering the signals as is done when covering an object in image classification tasks, because an empty region in a Mel-spectrogram does not necessarily mean it is "non-informative." After inspecting the histogram, we thought that separating Mel-spectrogram regions into signals and backgrounds using the value around the 2nd bin of the histograms could be useful, as it enables us to quantify how many tokens are retained in each category.

display_title: Official Review of Submission9332 by Reviewer VgML

summary.value: This paper investigates the application of token pruning in Vision Transformer (ViT)-based audio classification, a novel approach given that token pruning has predominantly been explored in image classification. The authors propose the Mean-Pooling EViT (MP-EViT) model, which applies token pruning to audio data represented as Mel-spectrograms. Their model successfully reduces computational costs—specifically, the multiply-accumulate operations (MACs)—by approximately 50%, while maintaining a high level of accuracy with only a minor loss (<1%) in performance. The authors demonstrate that, unlike in vision tasks where background tokens are frequently pruned, audio classification tasks require a more nuanced approach as both signal (high-intensity) and background (low-intensity) regions contribute significantly to classification accuracy. The paper’s contribution is the adaptation of token pruning techniques for audio tasks, providing insights into the behavior of ViT models in audio classification and highlighting the importance of background regions in this domain.

strengths.value:
1.Originality:
This paper presents an innovative application of token pruning within Vision Transformer (ViT)-based audio classification, specifically utilizing Mel-spectrograms as input data. While token pruning has been extensively explored in vision tasks, its application to audio tasks is relatively novel, providing new insights into how ViT models can handle non-visual data.
2.Quality:
The research is methodologically robust, supported by thorough experimental setups and well-designed ablation studies. 
3.Clarity:
The paper is clearly structured, with each section building upon the previous one to ensure that the readers can follow the motivations, methods, and analyses without ambiguity. 
4.Significance:
By extending token pruning to audio classification, this paper contributes to the broader research community by highlighting the potential of ViT models in diverse non-visual domains. The findings regarding the significant role of background tokens in audio classification provide a valuable perspective that may influence future research on feature importance within various data types.

weaknesses.value:
1.Limited Generalization Across Audio Tasks:
The experiments focus primarily on speech command recognition and environmental sound classification, which may limit the generalizability of the MP-EViT model to other types of audio classification tasks, such as speaker identification, music genre classification, or emotion recognition. 
2.Lack of Comparative Baselines:
While the paper compares the proposed MP-EViT model against the baseline without token pruning, it lacks comparisons with other state-of-the-art models or alternative token pruning methods adapted for audio tasks. For example, methods like DynamicViT and SPViT, which use prediction-based token pruning, could serve as useful comparisons to understand the relative benefits and limitations of the mean-pooling approach used here. This would clarify the advantages of MP-EViT relative to existing pruning techniques.

questions.value:
1.Generalizability of MP-EViT:
Could the authors elaborate on the potential limitations of applying MP-EViT to other audio classification tasks beyond speech command recognition and environmental sound classification? Have they considered tasks like speaker identification or music genre classification, which may involve different types of audio features? Expanding the evaluation to these tasks would provide a clearer picture of MP-EViT’s adaptability and robustness.
2.Comparative Baselines:
MP-EViT is evaluated mainly against a non-pruned baseline. Could the authors include comparisons with other token pruning methods adapted for audio, to give readers a broader context of the model’s performance? This would highlight MP-EViT’s unique advantages and any areas where other pruning methods may outperform it.

For AudioSet-20K, the mean Average Precision (mAP) decreased by approximately 0.005 for every 0.1 reduction in the keep-rate, until it reached a keep-rate of 0.6.

2. Comparative Baselines: MP-EViT is evaluated mainly against a non-pruned baseline. Could the authors include comparisons with other token pruning methods adapted for audio, to give readers a broader context of the model’s performance? This would highlight MP-EViT’s unique advantages and any areas where other pruning methods may outperform it.

* To the best of our knowledge, our work is the first work to apply token pruning on audio classification tasks.
* Instead, we added another experiment result with AST, which is pretrained on AudioSet-2M. Unlike AudioMAE results, AST gives much higher attention scores to the signal tokens than to the background token. And the pruning patterns of AudioMAE and AST are notably different; AST gives more attention scores to signal tokens than to background tokens. We added detailed comparison including visualization results to the appendix of our revised paper. 
* This difference can be attributed to their pretraining objectives: In AudioMAE, the model processes audio by considering not only signal but also background tokens, as all patches are masked during training. In contrast, AST focuses primarily on signal tokens with higher intensity values. This distinction can lead to different pruning behaviors: AudioMAE-TopK pruning retains both signal and background tokens for classification tasks, while AST-TopK pruning primarily preserves signal tokens.

summary.value: In this paper authors propose to prune blocks from the ViT when processing audio mel-spec data thus improving the computational efficiency without too much effect on the performance.

strengths.value:
Potentially useful way to process large audio corpora with this setup. ViT is useful in when first considering mel-spec as an image and then progressing as it would be an image. So the complete ViT pipeline for images would be applicable. Removing unnecessary blocks is reasonable as not every pixel in mel-spec is useful. 

Extensive ablation tests on the proposed method are clearly a positive side of this work.

We appreciate your review. Below are our responds to questions.

1. Empirical comparisons to other published works is the main problem in this work. Authors do explain multiple different ways to improve computational efficiency (for images) and also for audio all using the ViT framework as far as I can decode.

* In response to your comment, we provide a more comprehensive exploration of baseline audio classification models and pruning criteria used in other published works.
* First of all, we renamed our model from MP-EViT to AudioMAE-TopK to clarify the type of baseline model we use and its pruning methods.
* During the rebuttal phase, we added experiments with AST, pretrained with supervised learning,  to see if we observe the similar results from AudioMAE-TopK. To find out whether the final summarization method can impact the behavior of an audio model, we downloaded a model using CLS token (AST-TopK-CLS) and also pretrained an AST model using mean pooling to predict the label using AudioSet-2M (AST-TopK-MP).
* Interestingly, when token pruning is applied, AST-TopK retains more signal tokens than background tokens unlike AudioMAE-TopK, regardless of using a CLS token or mean pooling. Also, signal tokens get more attention scores than background tokens in AST-TopK.
* We think this difference can be attributed to their pre-training objectives: In AudioMAE, the model processes audio by considering not only signal but also background tokens, as all patches are masked during training. In contrast, AST focuses primarily on signal tokens with higher intensity values. This distinction can lead to different pruning behaviors: AudioMAE-TopK pruning retains both signal and background tokens for classification tasks, while AST-TopK pruning retains more signal tokens.
* We also have considered using other audio models using window or grid attention but they disrupt the direct mapping between tokens and their corresponding regions in the Mel spectrogram, making them unsuitable for our ablation studies.
* We appreciate your review to help us find the other pruning behaviors using different models.

2. Reading the title I was expecting to see something where peculiarities of spectrogram (or mel-spec as it is compressed spectrogram) would be utilized to improve the pruning. But I really do not see anything of the sort, I hope authors can clarify this in the rebuttal stage. It is noteworthy that even though a spectrogram is an image it is a very structured image, y-axis refers to frequency and x-axis refers to time, so for example in speech processing only a slice of the spectrogram would contain useful content. And in detail, speech spectrograms have a peculiar structure with harmonic and non-harmonic portions (such as 'a' has harmonics, whereas 's' not so much).


* As you recommended, we believe that using audio-specific features like harmonic or non-harmonic portions can provide hints for which tokens are retained or pruned. (e.g., the Swin Transformer used prior knowledge of locality in image tasks). We reflected your feedback at the end of the discussion in our revised paper.
* We are currently exploring the importance of harmonic/non-harmonic portions in token pruning. We look forward to uploading additional findings during the rebuttal session. We appreciate your feedback; it has brought new insights to us.

metareview.value:
This paper investigates the application of token pruning to Masked Auto-Encoder based audio classification, a slightly novel investigation given that token pruning has predominantly been explored in image classification. The authors propose the AudioMAE-TopK (called Mean-Pooling EViT, MP-EViT, in the first version of the paper) model, which applies token pruning to audio data represented as Mel-spectrograms. The model successfully reduces computational costs—specifically, the multiply-accumulate operations (MACs)—by approximately 50%, while maintaining a high level of accuracy with only a minor loss (<1%) in performance. The authors demonstrate that, unlike in vision tasks where "background tokens" are frequently pruned in ViT, audio classification tasks (where ViT is called Audio MAE) require a more nuanced approach as there are no real "signal" (high-intensity) and "background" (low-intensity) regions, which can be pruned without affecting downstream performance. 

Strengths
- the paper presents a large number of experimental results with detailed analysis - supporting our understanding of how audio data is different from image data while all the downstream processing (ViT/ AudioMAE) is the same
- authors engaged in a good discussion with reviewers which led some to increase their score, authors increased the strengths of the results by adding additional datasets (VoxCeleb-1 and AudioSet-20K) and analyzing a related model (AST)
- the paper is well written and experiments are sound

Weaknesses
- Novelty appears somewhat limited, the paper is mostly analytical and does not present a significant new technique that works better for audio (the number of tokens that can be pruned with the TopK method before performance degrades is small)

Overall, this is a borderline paper. I recommend acceptance since the analysis is insightful and well executed, and I think we should understand the data we work with, even if we always apply mostly the same models to the data now. However, if the paper cannot be accepted, publication at a venue such as ICASSP is a viable alternative.

additional_comments_on_reviewer_discussi.value: Reviewers made several good comments (suggesting renaming to AudioMAE), asked for additional experiments, which the authors responded positively to. This raised the quality of the paper and the reviewers' perception.

Dear research community, 

While preparing our code for public release to facilitate reproducibility, we identified a mistake that significantly impacts Sections 4 and 5 of our paper, which analyze the token pruning behavior of AudioMAE (our audio classification model).

We outline the details of our error below:

* Our analysis for identifying retained tokens in the token pruning process of AudioMAE relied on extracting Top-K indices from the transformer’s attention modules.
* Regrettably, we mistakenly applied the function [random_masking_2d()](https://github.com/facebookresearch/AudioMAE/blob/bd60e29651285f80d32a6405082835ad26e6f19f/models_vit.py#L89) during our model analysis. We failed to recognize that this function not only performs masking but also shuffles tokens regardless of the specified masking probability. Consequently, even when we set masking probability to 0 in our experiments, token shuffling still occurred. This resulted in a mismatch between the token indices and the corresponding parts of the mel-spectrogram, leading us to erroneously conclude that a significant portion of background tokens were retained relative to signal tokens. Our fixed implementation shows AudioMAE retains much more signal tokens than background tokens like AST, which contradicts our original claim.
* Despite observing unusual visualization patterns due to the mismatch, our model's accuracy appeared unaffected, leading us to mistakenly believe the implementation was correct.
* The experiment presented in Section 5.3 involving the AST remains valid since we followed the training parameters of the original paper, which does not include token shuffling.

Lastly, we sincerely apologize to all the readers, reviewers, program and area chairs, and the research community for the confusion and inconvenience caused by our errors.

Sincerely, Authors
